[.note: This is the coreutils test command under another name. Bash also provides [ as a builtin, so type [ before you trust a flag. The manual lists it among utilities whose exit status is the answer, not a simple success bit.

arch.note: Prints the machine hardware name, the same class of fact as uname -m. It is a tiny GNU program. macOS often has no arch from coreutils; uname -m is the portable question.

b2sum.note: BLAKE2b checksums with the same check-file interface as sha256sum. A faster median than SHA-256 on one host is not a reason to change a manifest format. Length can be shortened with -l; do that only when the consumer expects it.

base32.note: RFC 4648 base32. GNU base32 wraps at 76 columns unless -w 0. Decode with -d. It is not on stock macOS; basenc --base32 is the same alphabet inside coreutils.

base64.note: RFC 4648 base64. -w sets the wrap column and -d decodes. macOS base64 uses -D and a different default wrap. Whitespace on decode needs -i. This is encoding, not encryption.

basename.note: Strips the directory prefix and an optional trailing suffix. It reads operands, not stdin. GNU basename accepts -a and -z. Quoting still matters because the shell expands the argument first.

basenc.note: One binary for base16, base32, base32hex, base64, base64url, base2msbf, base2lsbf, and z85 in coreutils 9.4. There is no --base58 in this version. z85 input length must be a multiple of 4.

cat.note: Streams files to stdout. -A shows tabs, ends, and other nonprinting bytes. The manual says cat does not use C FILE streams, so stdbuf does not change its buffering. It is the wrong tool for random access.

chcon.note: Changes an SELinux security context. This capture host has no SELinux-enabled kernel, and chcon fails on unlabeled files. Do not treat a failure here as a permissions-bit problem; chmod is a different mechanism.

chgrp.note: Changes group ownership. Without privilege you can only move a file to a group you belong to. --reference copies the group from another file. BSD chgrp does not take GNU long options.

chmod.note: Changes mode bits with an octal mode or a symbolic mode. --reference copies a mode. It does not change the owner. Recursive -R on a tree you do not mean to publish is the usual accident.

chown.note: Changes user and group. On this sandbox, chown to root fails with Operation not permitted. --from avoids racing with another owner. GNU --reference is not a BSD flag.

cksum.note: The historical CRC plus byte count is still the default. -a selects md5, the SHA-2 family, blake2b, sm3, and the old sum algorithms. --tag is how cryptographic digests print a BSD-style line; the CRC line stays numeric.

comm.note: Compares two sorted files line by line and prints three columns. GNU comm checks order and exits 1 when it is wrong, after it may already have written lines. Suppress columns with -1, -2, and -3.

cp.note: Copies files and trees. -a is -dR --preserve=all. --reflink=always fails on this ext4 filesystem; --reflink=auto falls back to a read/write copy. --sparse controls holes. -n is marked non-portable in 9.4; use --update=none.

csplit.note: Splits a file at context lines rather than at a fixed size. Patterns are basic regular expressions. -z suppresses empty pieces. It is not a CSV or JSON parser. Stock macOS does not ship GNU csplit.

cut.note: Selects byte, character, or field ranges. -d sets a single-byte delimiter. It does not understand quotes, so a CSV comma inside quotes is still a separator. --complement and --output-delimiter are GNU extensions.

date.note: Formats and parses dates. -d takes a date string, including @epoch. BSD date uses -v and -f instead. --debug explains a parse. The clock resolution reported by --resolution is a property of this host.

dd.note: Copies blocks. status=progress and status=none are GNU. conv=sparse seeks over NUL blocks. iflag=fullblock matters when reading a pipe that returns short reads. Never point of= at a device in an example you have not identified.

df.note: Reports filesystem free space from statfs, not by walking files. GNU df -T prints the type. On BSD, df -T filters by type instead. --output and -T cannot be combined. This host's df -T says ext4 where stat -f says ext2/ext3.

dir.note: dir is ls with a different default format, still the same coreutils binary family. Scripts should call ls with explicit options so a dir default never becomes part of the contract.

dircolors.note: Prints shell commands that set LS_COLORS. The database is not consulted unless the shell evaluates that output. Color is a display hint. It does not change the bytes ls writes when --color=never.

dirname.note: Prints everything through the last slash. Multiple operands are allowed. -z changes the output delimiter; it does not make dirname read NUL-separated stdin. A path with no slash yields '.'.

du.note: Walks a tree and sums allocated space, counting a hard link once unless -l is set. --apparent-size or -b reports the logical size, which is what sparse files make diverge from du without that flag. df does not walk the tree.

echo.note: The manual recommends printf for anything that must be portable. Bash's builtin echo ignores --help and prints the word. /usr/bin/echo is coreutils, and -E (no escapes) is its default. -e is a GNU behavior, not POSIX.

env.note: Runs a command with a modified environment. -i starts empty, -u removes a name, -C changes directory, and -S splits a string for shebangs. The manual lists env among commands with special exit statuses. BSD env lacks -S.

expand.note: Turns tabs into spaces. -t sets tab stops. -i affects only leading tabs. It does not reflow paragraphs; fmt does that. Tabs inside the data are bytes, not a table layout.

expr.note: Evaluates an expression and prints it. A true comparison prints 1 and exits 0. A false comparison prints 0 and exits 1. That inversion surprises people who treat the printed number as the exit status. Prefer test or shell arithmetic for new scripts.

factor.note: Prints prime factors of arbitrary-precision integers. factor 1 and factor 0 print the number and no factors. It is not a general cryptography library and it is not a reason to invent timing claims.

false.note: Exits with status 1. Bash also has a builtin false. /usr/bin/false --version identifies coreutils. The manual lists false as an ordinary failure status, unlike test's use of 1 as an answer.

fmt.note: Reflows paragraphs to a width. -w sets the width and -p keeps a mail-style prefix. It is not a code formatter and it will join short lines that look like a paragraph. BSD fmt exists with a different option set.

fold.note: Wraps lines at a width. On this UTF-8 locale, fold -w 1 split the two bytes of U+00E9. Do not assume a column width keeps a multibyte character intact; check with od. -b counts bytes. -s breaks at spaces.

groups.note: Prints the groups of a user. With no operand it describes the current process. It reads the account database, not the file mode bits. id -Gn is the related coreutils form.

head.note: Prints a prefix. GNU head -n -5 prints all but the last five lines; BSD head rejects a negative count. -c counts bytes. -z uses NUL as the line delimiter. It does not follow a growing file; tail -f does.

hostid.note: Prints a hexadecimal identifier, historically derived from an address. It is not a UUID and not a secret you should publish as an authenticator. Treat the captured value as a fact about this machine only.

id.note: Prints uid, gid, and groups. -u and -g print numbers. -Z asks for an SELinux context and fails on this kernel. Scripts that parse the default sentence are brittle; use the numeric options.

install.note: Copies a file and sets its mode, creating parent directories with -D. -C skips the write when the content already matches, which keeps the destination mtime. BSD install uses a different flag set. It is the right tool for placing a built binary into a prefix.

join.note: Joins two files on a shared field. Both inputs must be sorted on that field. The default GNU check exits 1 on disorder but can still emit a partial line. --nocheck-order returns 0 and can silently drop rows.

link.note: Creates a hard link with link(2) and no extra flags. It will not replace an existing name and it will not link a directory for an unprivileged user. ln is the tool with -s, -f, and -r. unlink is the matching removal call.

ln.note: Makes hard and symbolic links. -s is a symlink. GNU -r / --relative rewrites the target as a relative path. -sfn retargets a symlink even when the destination name exists. BSD ln has no --relative.

logname.note: Prints the name from the login utmp record. In this non-login sandbox it fails. whoami reads the effective uid instead and still works. Do not use logname as a synonym for the account that owns the files.

ls.note: Lists names and, with -l, metadata. The shell expands globs before ls sees them. --quoting-style=shell-escape makes odd names visible. --zero delimits with NUL. GNU -T is tab size; BSD ls -T is a time format. dir and vdir are related entry points.

md5sum.note: MD5 checksums in the GNU text/binary line format. Fine for accidental corruption checks in old manifests. Not a collision-resistant choice for new ones. --check and --status match the other *sum tools. md5sum.textutils is a symlink, not a second algorithm.

mkdir.note: Creates directories. -p creates parents and does not fail if the leaf exists. -m applies to the final component created in that invocation; parents are created under the current umask, which is 0022 here, so they land at 755 when -m 700 is asked.

mkfifo.note: Creates a named pipe. Opening it blocks until the other end is opened. A lesson that reads a fifo must bound the wait with timeout, or the sandbox hangs. mkfifo does not copy bytes; the readers and writers do.

mknod.note: Creates fifos, and device nodes when you pass a type and numbers. Device nodes need privileges this course does not use. Prefer mkfifo for a named pipe. Do not run mknod against /dev in examples.

mktemp.note: Creates a temporary file or directory with a unique name. The template must end in at least six X characters. -d makes a directory. --suffix appends a suffix after the X's. Leaving the default /tmp is fine; the course scripts also set TMPDIR to the sandbox.

mv.note: Renames, or copies and unlinks when the destination is another filesystem. -n refuses to overwrite and, on this GNU version, exits 1. -t collects sources into a directory. There is no cross-device rename system call; EXDEV is why the copy happens.

nice.note: Adjusts niceness and runs a command. The manual says a negative adjustment without privilege prints a warning and continues as if the adjustment were zero. The exit status is the command's status, not the warning. renice is a different program and is not coreutils.

nl.note: Numbers lines. -ba is -b a, which numbers every line including blanks. The default body style skips blanks. It is a formatter, not a way to address lines for editing. BSD nl differs in style names.

nohup.note: Runs a command immune to SIGHUP and, if stdout is a terminal, redirects it to nohup.out. When stdout is already redirected, nohup.out is not created. It does not daemonize, and it does not change niceness.

nproc.note: Prints the number of processing units available to the process, which can be less than --all when the affinity mask is smaller. --ignore subtracts from that count. GNU documents the default sort --parallel cap in terms of available processors. nproc is not in BSD base.

numfmt.note: Formats numbers with SI or IEC suffixes. 2048 becomes 2.0K in IEC (1024) and 2.1K in SI (1000) because of rounding. --field selects a column. It is GNU-only. It does not change sort's numeric comparison; sort -h has its own rules.

od.note: Dumps bytes in hex, octal, or named characters. Use it when cat -A is not enough, especially for NULs and encoding mistakes. -An drops the address. -w sets the width. hexdump is a different program and is not coreutils.

paste.note: Merges lines from files, or, with -s, joins lines of one file. -d sets the delimiter. -z uses NUL as the record separator. It does not sort or match keys; join does that.

pathchk.note: Checks whether a name is portable. -p applies the POSIX portable character set and a length limit. A name containing | fails -p. It does not create the file and it does not tell you whether the directory is writable.

pinky.note: A lightweight who. With nobody recorded in utmp it prints a header and no rows, which is what this sandbox shows. It is GNU-specific. who reads the same kind of login records.

pr.note: Paginates and columns text. -t drops the header and footer so the output can go to another filter. -s sets a column separator. It is not a table join. Default headers include the date, so scripts that need stable bytes pass -t.

printenv.note: Prints the environment or one variable. A missing name exits non-zero, which the manual calls out. -0 uses NUL delimiters. env runs a command; printenv only displays.

printf.note: Formats operands. Bash also has a builtin printf. Use /usr/bin/printf when you need the coreutils binary, including %q for shell quoting. The format string is not a filename. Prefer printf over echo for escapes and missing newlines.

ptx.note: Builds a permuted index. It is a specialized text tool, not a sort replacement. The output columns are easy to misread; the manual's ptx section documents the format. Most developer workflows never need it.

pwd.note: Prints the working directory. Bash's builtin pwd is what you get if you type pwd. /usr/bin/pwd is coreutils. -P resolves symlinks; -L follows the logical $PWD. The builtin and the binary agree on this sandbox because the directory is not reached through a link.

readlink.note: Prints the target of a symlink, or, with -f, a canonical path. -f allows the final component to be missing and still exits 0. -e requires every component to exist. GNU -f is not what older BSD readlink implemented.

realpath.note: Prints an absolute path. The default allows a missing final component. -e requires the path to exist. -m allows missing middle components. --relative-to prints a path relative to a base. Older macOS installs did not ship realpath.

rm.note: Removes directory entries. GNU defaults include --preserve-root. -I prompts once before removing more than three items or descending recursively; an EOF answer left the files in place and still exited 0 in this sandbox. -i prompts per file. It does not shred data.

rmdir.note: Removes empty directories. A non-empty directory and a regular file both fail, with different messages. -p removes parent components if they become empty. Use rm -r only when you mean to delete contents.

runcon.note: Runs a command in a different SELinux context. It needs a kernel with SELinux. This host does not have one. It is not a substitute for sudo and not a coreutils permission bit.

seq.note: Prints a sequence of numbers. -w equalizes width and -s sets the separator. The floating-point section of the manual applies. On 9.4, seq 0 0.1 1 prints 11 values ending at 1.0 for this particular step; that is not a proof that every step is exact.

sha1sum.note: SHA-1 checksums, 160-bit, same interface as sha256sum. Collision attacks against SHA-1 are practical. Do not choose it for a new manifest. The manual groups it with the SHA-2 tools even though SHA-1 is not SHA-2.

sha224sum.note: SHA-224, a truncated SHA-256 variant with a different initial state. Same -c interface. Rare in download pages. Prefer sha256sum unless a protocol names SHA-224.

sha256sum.note: SHA-256 checksums. This is the usual coreutils tool for a download manifest. --check reads the GNU line format. A wrong hash prints FAILED and exits 1. The digest of the three bytes abc is a known test vector used in the lesson.

sha384sum.note: SHA-384, the truncated SHA-512 variant. Same command-line shape as sha256sum. Choose it when a protocol says SHA-384, not because the name looks longer than SHA-256.

sha512sum.note: SHA-512. The digest is longer and the implementation processes 64-bit words. On a small file the runtime difference may sit inside the noise. Use the benchmark if you need a number, and do not generalize it.

shred.note: Overwrites a file, and -u unlinks it afterward. The manual's assumption is that the filesystem and the device overwrite in place. Journals, snapshots, compression, RAID, and SSD wear leveling break that assumption. One pass in a lesson only shows the user interface.

shuf.note: Writes a random permutation. There is no --seed. Reproducible draws use --random-source with a file of bytes. -i ranges over integers and -n limits the count. shuf is GNU-only; it is not a sort.

sleep.note: Pauses for a duration. GNU sleep accepts a decimal and the suffixes s, m, h, and d. An invalid interval exits non-zero. It is not a scheduler. timeout is the tool that stops another command.

sort.note: Orders lines. -s disables the last-resort full-line comparison. -S sets the initial memory buffer (default unit 1024 bytes; M is 1,048,576). -T sets the temporary directory. --parallel defaults to available CPUs capped at 8. Exit status 1 means a -c check failed; 2 means an error.

split.note: Splits by lines, bytes, or into N chunks. -d uses numeric suffixes. -n r/N round-robins lines, so a file with one line puts everything in the first piece. --filter runs a command per piece. BSD split does not have this -n syntax.

stat.note: Prints metadata with a format string. GNU uses -c. BSD uses -f for the format, which is the single most common portability break. stat -f here means filesystem status, and %T can say ext2/ext3 on ext4.

stdbuf.note: Adjusts C FILE buffering by preloading libstdbuf.so. The binary contains the strings LD_PRELOAD and libstdbuf.so. cat and dd do not use FILE streams. tee resets its own buffering. -iL is rejected with status 125. It is ELF-only and GNU-only.

stty.note: Changes or prints terminal settings. This course does not run stty against the session terminal, because a bad mode breaks the terminal. Read the manual before using it in a script. It is not a file-permission tool.

sum.note: Historic BSD (-r) and System V (-s) checksums. cksum -a bsd and cksum -a sysv cover the same algorithms. Do not use sum for a new integrity check. The output width and algorithm differ between -r and -s.

sync.note: Asks the kernel to flush cached writes. With no operand it syncs all filesystems the process may sync. -f syncs the filesystems that contain the named files. It does not prove a drive's firmware finished the write.

tac.note: Prints lines in reverse. It is GNU-only; BSD users often use tail -r. -s sets a separator, and the separator stays attached to the record, which makes the reversed bytes look surprising until you inspect them with od.

tail.note: Prints a suffix, or follows a file with -f. -F follows by name and retries. -n +K starts at line K. GNU negative counts on head are a different feature. Follow mode runs until it is killed; bound it with timeout.

tee.note: Copies stdin to stdout and to files. -a appends. The manual notes that tee adjusts its own buffering, so stdbuf does not control it. It is the coreutils way to save a copy of a pipeline without a shell process substitution.

test.note: Evaluates an expression and exits 0 or 1. Bash's builtin test shadows /usr/bin/test. -s is true only for a non-empty file. The manual lists test among the commands whose 0 and 1 are answers. Use spaces around operators.

timeout.note: Runs a command and sends it a signal when the duration elapses. The default exit status is 124 if the command was signaled. --preserve-status returns 128 plus the signal, 143 for SIGTERM. It is GNU-only. macOS users install gtimeout.

touch.note: Updates timestamps or creates an empty file. -d takes a date string and -r copies a timestamp from another file. -c does not create. BSD touch uses -t for a timestamp and does not accept GNU -d.

tr.note: Translates or deletes bytes from stdin. It has no file operands. Character classes such as [:upper:] are locale-sensitive. A UTF-8 character is more than one byte, and tr will rewrite each byte that appears in the set. It is not sed.

true.note: Exits with status 0. The shell builtin is what an unadorned true usually runs. /usr/bin/true --version prints the coreutils banner. Useful as the command argument to nice or timeout when you need a known status.

truncate.note: Sets a file to a size. Extending a file creates a hole when the filesystem allows it, which is why du and stat then disagree. Shrinking discards the tail from the directory entry's point of view. It is GNU; it is not dd.

tsort.note: Topological order of a list of pairs. Input is one pair per line. A cycle makes it fail. It is the coreutils tool for a dependency order, not a general sort, and the input is not a Makefile.

tty.note: Prints the terminal name connected to stdin, or fails when stdin is not a terminal. Pipelines and this capture environment are not terminals, so tty exits non-zero. The manual lists tty among special exit statuses.

uname.note: Prints kernel and machine facts. -srm is enough to identify the capture class without a hostname. -a includes the nodename. It does not print the coreutils version; ls --version does that.

unexpand.note: Turns runs of spaces into tabs. -a converts all runs, not only leading ones. -t must match the tab stops expand used, or the round trip changes columns. It is byte-oriented.

uniq.note: Collapses adjacent matching lines. It does not search the whole file; sort first. -c counts, -d prints duplicates, -u prints uniques. -i folds case. GNU -z matches sort -z. sort -u is not the same once keys are involved.

unlink.note: Removes one name with unlink(2). It does not remove directories. It does not take -r. If another hard link remains, the data remains. rm is the tool with prompts and recursion.

users.note: Prints login names from utmp. This sandbox has no logged-in users, so the output is empty and the status is still 0. An empty line is not an error. who shows the same records with more columns.

vdir.note: vdir is ls -l under another name, from the same package. Use it only when you want that default. Scripts should call ls -l so the format is explicit on systems where vdir is absent.

wc.note: Counts newlines, words, characters, bytes, and the longest line. -l counts newline bytes, so a file with no trailing newline can have a last line that -l does not count. --files0-from reads NUL-separated names. --total controls the total line.

who.note: Prints utmp records. With no logins it prints nothing and exits 0. It is coreutils on this Ubuntu. uptime is not, even though people mention them together. Do not parse who to authorize a user.

whoami.note: Prints the effective user name. It still works when logname fails. It does not print the uid; id -u does. It is not a security boundary.

yes.note: Repeats a string until the pipe closes. The usual close is SIGPIPE. With pipefail the pipeline can exit 141. Without pipefail the status is the reader's status. Bound it with head. It is not a load generator you should leave running.
